name: War in Afghanistan
summary: After the 11 September 2001 attacks, a US-led coalition and Afghan Northern Alliance forces overthrew the Taliban government that had sheltered al-Qaeda. The Taliban regrouped and waged a long insurgency against the new Afghan government and NATO forces. After a 2020 US-Taliban deal, foreign troops withdrew and the Taliban retook the country in August 2021.

steps.label: Oct to Dec 2001
steps.title: The Taliban overthrown
steps.text: From 7 October US and British air strikes and special forces backed the Northern Alliance, which held only a strip of the northeast. Abdul Rashid Dostum took Mazar-i-Sharif on 9 November, Mohammed Fahim's forces entered Kabul on 13 November, and Hamid Karzai and Gul Agha Sherzai closed on Kandahar, which fell in early December. Osama bin Laden escaped from Tora Bora into Pakistan.

moves.label: From the Pakistan border to Kandahar

events.name: Fall of Mazar-i-Sharif
events.text: The first major city to fall opened a land route from Uzbekistan.

events.name: Fall of Kabul
events.text: Taliban forces abandoned the capital on 13 November.

events.name: Battle of Tora Bora
events.text: Al-Qaeda's mountain stronghold was overrun, but bin Laden escaped.

steps.label: 2002 to 2005
steps.title: A new government
steps.text: The Bonn Agreement made Hamid Karzai interim leader, and a NATO-led force (ISAF) secured Kabul and later spread across the country. In March 2002 US forces fought al-Qaeda and Taliban fighters in the Shah-i-Kot valley, and the remaining leaders withdrew into Pakistan's border regions. Karzai won Afghanistan's first presidential election in 2004.

events.name: Bonn Agreement
events.text: Afghan factions agreed on an interim government led by Karzai.

events.name: Operation Anaconda
events.text: US and allied troops cleared the valley after heavy fighting, but many fighters slipped away.

events.name: Presidential election
events.text: Karzai was elected president in October 2004.

steps.label: 2006 to 2008
steps.title: The Taliban return in the south
steps.text: As NATO extended its mission into the south, the Taliban, directed by leaders based in Pakistan, launched a large insurgency in Kandahar and Helmand. Canadian-led troops fought Operation Medusa west of Kandahar, and British forces in Helmand were drawn into long fights for district centres such as Sangin and Musa Qala. Roadside bombs and suicide attacks spread across the country.

moves.label: Taliban push into Kandahar and Helmand

events.name: Operation Medusa
events.text: NATO's largest combat operation to date drove Taliban fighters out of Panjwai district.

events.name: Battle of Musa Qala
events.text: Afghan and British troops retook the town the Taliban had held since early 2007.

steps.label: 2009 to 2011
steps.title: The surge
steps.text: President Obama sent about 30,000 more troops, and commanders Stanley McChrystal and then David Petraeus pursued a counterinsurgency campaign focused on Helmand and Kandahar. US Marines took Marja in February 2010, and later offensives cleared districts around Kandahar. On 2 May 2011 US special forces killed Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad, Pakistan.

events.name: Battle of Marja
events.text: Marines and Afghan troops seized the Taliban-held farming district.

events.name: Death of Osama bin Laden
events.text: The al-Qaeda leader was killed in a night raid on his compound.

steps.label: 2014 to 2016
steps.title: Afghan forces take the lead
steps.text: Ashraf Ghani became president in 2014, and NATO ended its combat mission in December, leaving a smaller training force. The Taliban, led from 2015 by Akhtar Mansour and from 2016 by Haibatullah Akhundzada, gained ground in the countryside. In September 2015 they briefly captured the northern city of Kunduz before Afghan forces with US air support retook it.

events.name: End of ISAF combat mission
events.text: NATO handed security to Afghan forces and began the smaller Resolute Support mission.

events.name: Battle of Kunduz
events.text: The Taliban held the city for about two weeks, their biggest gain since 2001.

steps.label: 2018 to 2020
steps.title: Talks with the Taliban
steps.text: With the war in stalemate and the Taliban contesting much of the countryside, the United States opened direct talks led by Zalmay Khalilzad. The Doha Agreement of 29 February 2020 committed the US to withdraw its troops in exchange for Taliban security guarantees, and intra-Afghan talks began that September without result.

events.name: Battle of Ghazni
events.text: Taliban fighters overran much of the city for several days before being driven out.

events.name: Doha Agreement
events.text: The US agreed to a full withdrawal; the Afghan government was not a party.

steps.label: May to Aug 2021
steps.title: The fall of Kabul
steps.text: As US and NATO troops withdrew, a Taliban offensive took rural districts and border crossings, then the provincial capitals in quick succession in August. Kabul fell on 15 August as President Ghani left the country. A US-led airlift evacuated over 120,000 people, a suicide bombing by the Islamic State's local branch killed about 170 Afghans and 13 US troops at the airport, and the last US forces left on 30 August.

events.name: Fall of Kabul
events.text: The Taliban entered the capital without a fight on 15 August.

events.name: Kabul airport bombing
events.text: An Islamic State suicide attack hit crowds at the airport gates on 26 August.

events.name: Last US flight leaves
events.text: The final US aircraft departed on 30 August, ending the 20-year war.

name: Iraq War
summary: A US-led coalition invaded Iraq in March 2003 and overthrew Saddam Hussein, citing weapons of mass destruction that were never found. The occupation faced a growing insurgency and a sectarian civil war, which eased after the 2007 troop surge and the Sunni Awakening. US forces left at the end of 2011, but the Islamic State's rise in 2014 brought renewed war until 2017.

sides.name: US-led coalition and new Iraqi government
Saddam Hussein's government, then insurgent groups

steps.label: Mar to Apr 2003
steps.title: Invasion
steps.text: On 20 March 2003 coalition forces under Tommy Franks crossed from Kuwait. The US Army's V Corps raced up the Euphrates past Najaf and through the Karbala Gap, US Marines advanced through Nasiriyah and Kut, and British troops took Basra. Baghdad fell on 9 April, and Saddam Hussein went into hiding.

fronts.label: Front south of Baghdad, early Apr 2003

moves.commander: US special forces and Kurdish Peshmerga
moves.label: Northern front to Kirkuk

events.name: Battle of Nasiriyah
events.text: Marines fought through the city to secure the Euphrates bridges.

events.name: Battle of Basra
events.text: British forces entered Iraq's second city after a two-week siege.

events.name: Fall of Baghdad
events.text: US troops entered the capital and Saddam's government collapsed on 9 April.

steps.label: 2003 to 2004
steps.title: Occupation and insurgency
steps.text: The Coalition Provisional Authority under Paul Bremer disbanded the army and purged Ba'ath party members, and a mainly Sunni insurgency grew alongside Abu Musab al-Zarqawi's jihadist network. US troops captured Saddam near Tikrit in December 2003. In 2004 Muqtada al-Sadr's Mahdi Army rose in Najaf, sovereignty passed to an interim Iraqi government, and US Marines stormed Fallujah in November.

events.name: Capture of Saddam Hussein
events.text: He was found hiding near ad-Dawr on 13 December and executed in 2006.

events.name: Second Battle of Fallujah
events.text: US and Iraqi troops retook the insurgent-held city in the war's heaviest urban fighting.

steps.label: 2005 to 2006
steps.title: Sectarian civil war
steps.text: Iraqis voted in elections and approved a new constitution in 2005, but Sunni-Shia violence soared after the bombing of the al-Askari shrine in Samarra in February 2006. Militias and death squads killed thousands of civilians a month in and around Baghdad. Zarqawi was killed in a US air strike in June 2006, but his group, al-Qaeda in Iraq, carried on.

events.name: Samarra mosque bombing
events.text: The destruction of the Shia shrine's golden dome set off a wave of sectarian killings.

events.name: Death of al-Zarqawi
events.text: The al-Qaeda in Iraq leader was killed in an air strike near Baqubah.

steps.label: 2007 to 2008
steps.title: Surge and Awakening
steps.text: President Bush sent about 30,000 more troops under David Petraeus to secure Baghdad, while Sunni tribes in Anbar, the Awakening, turned against al-Qaeda in Iraq. In March 2008 Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki sent the Iraqi army against Shia militias in Basra and later Sadr City. Violence fell sharply, and in November 2008 Iraq and the US agreed that US troops would leave by the end of 2011.

events.name: Anbar Awakening
events.text: Sunni tribal leaders around Ramadi allied with US forces against al-Qaeda in Iraq.

events.name: Battle of Basra
events.text: Iraqi forces regained control of the city from Mahdi Army fighters.

events.name: Status of Forces Agreement
events.text: The deal set the withdrawal of all US forces by 31 December 2011.

steps.label: 2009 to 2011
steps.title: US withdrawal
steps.text: US troops left Iraqi cities in June 2009 and ended combat operations in August 2010, leaving advisers under Ray Odierno and then Lloyd Austin. Political deadlock and attacks continued, but Iraqi forces took over security. The last US troops crossed into Kuwait on 18 December 2011.

events.name: End of US combat mission
events.text: Operation Iraqi Freedom became Operation New Dawn, an advisory mission.

events.name: Last US troops leave
events.text: The final convoy crossed the border on 18 December 2011.

steps.label: 2011 to 2017, aftermath
steps.title: Rise and fall of the Islamic State
steps.text: Remnants of al-Qaeda in Iraq, rebuilt as the Islamic State under Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, grew during the Syrian civil war and in Sunni discontent with the Maliki government. In June 2014 they seized Mosul and drove toward Baghdad, and Baghdadi declared a caliphate. Iraqi forces, Kurdish Peshmerga, Shia militias and a US-led air campaign took the territory back, ending with Mosul in July 2017.

fronts.label: Approx. edge of Islamic State territory, late 2014

events.name: Fall of Mosul
events.text: A small Islamic State force routed the much larger Iraqi garrison in June 2014.

events.name: Battle of Mosul
events.text: Nine months of urban fighting ended with the city's recapture in July 2017.

name: Mexican Drug War
summary: In December 2006 President Felipe Calderon deployed the army against Mexico's drug-trafficking organisations, which also fought each other for smuggling routes into the United States. Arrests and killings of kingpins fragmented the cartels and spread violence across the country, with hundreds of thousands killed or missing since 2006. Successive governments changed strategy, but the conflict continued at the end of 2025.

steps.label: 2006 to 2007
steps.title: The army is sent in
steps.text: Days after taking office in December 2006, Felipe Calderon sent thousands of soldiers and federal police into his home state of Michoacan, then to Guerrero, Baja California and the northern border states. The campaign targeted the leaders of the Sinaloa, Gulf, Juarez and Tijuana organisations and La Familia Michoacana.

events.name: Operation Michoacan
events.text: About 6,500 troops and police opened the government offensive on 11 December 2006.

steps.label: 2008 to 2010
steps.title: Cartel wars on the border
steps.text: The Sinaloa cartel under Joaquin Guzman fought the Juarez cartel for Ciudad Juarez, which became one of the most violent cities in the world. In 2010 Los Zetas broke from the Gulf cartel, setting off a war across Tamaulipas and the northeast. The US Merida Initiative funded equipment and training for Mexican forces.

moves.label: Los Zetas against the Gulf cartel

events.name: Battle for Ciudad Juarez
events.text: Thousands were killed in the city between 2008 and 2011 as cartels fought and the army deployed.

events.name: San Fernando massacre
events.text: Los Zetas killed 72 migrants in Tamaulipas in August 2010.

events.name: Death of Arturo Beltran Leyva
events.text: Marines killed the cartel leader in Cuernavaca in December 2009.

steps.label: 2011 to 2012
steps.title: Peak of the Calderon years
steps.text: Killings related to organised crime reached their first peak in 2011 as Los Zetas spread from the northeast to Veracruz and Coahuila. Mass attacks, such as the arson of a casino in Monterrey, shocked the country. In October 2012 marines killed Zetas leader Heriberto Lazcano in Coahuila.

events.name: Monterrey casino attack
events.text: An arson attack blamed on Los Zetas killed 52 people in August 2011.

events.name: Death of Heriberto Lazcano
events.text: The Zetas founder was killed in a firefight with marines in Coahuila.

steps.label: 2013 to 2018
steps.title: Kingpins fall, cartels splinter
steps.text: President Enrique Pena Nieto continued the pursuit of top leaders. Armed self-defence groups rose against the Knights Templar in Michoacan, and Joaquin Guzman was captured in 2014, escaped in 2015, was recaptured in 2016 and was extradited to the United States. The disappearance of 43 students in Iguala in 2014 caused national outrage, while the Jalisco New Generation Cartel grew into a major power.

events.name: Iguala disappearances
events.text: Forty-three students from Ayotzinapa disappeared after an attack involving police and a local gang.

events.name: Recapture of El Chapo
events.text: Marines caught Guzman in Los Mochis six months after his tunnel escape from prison.

steps.label: 2019 to 2024
steps.title: Hugs, not bullets
steps.text: President Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador promised to tackle the causes of violence and created a militarised National Guard, as homicides stayed near record levels. In October 2019 troops released Ovidio Guzman after cartel gunmen besieged Culiacan, then captured him in 2023. In July 2024 Ismael Zambada was taken to the United States, and the Sinaloa cartel split into a violent war between his faction and Guzman's sons.

events.name: Culiacan siege
events.text: The government freed Ovidio Guzman after armed attacks across the city.

events.name: Zambada taken to the US
events.text: His arrest near El Paso set off fighting inside the Sinaloa cartel.

steps.title: A new government, the same war
steps.text: Claudia Sheinbaum took office in October 2024 promising more intelligence-led policing, and her government reported a fall in homicides during 2025. Under pressure from the United States, which designated several cartels as terrorist organisations, Mexico sent dozens of jailed cartel figures to US courts. Violence remained high in Sinaloa, Guanajuato, Michoacan and other states.

events.name: Transfers to the United States
events.text: Mexico sent dozens of cartel prisoners to the US in 2025, including Rafael Caro Quintero.

name: Syrian Civil War
summary: Protests against Bashar al-Assad in 2011 met a violent crackdown and turned into a multi-sided war between the government, rebel groups, the Islamic State and Kurdish-led forces, drawing in Russia, Iran, Turkey and a US-led coalition. Russian and Iranian support let Assad recover most cities by 2018, and front lines froze in 2020. In late 2024 a rebel offensive led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham took Damascus and ended the Assad government.

sides.name: Assad government and allies (Russia, Iran, Hezbollah)
Rebel opposition (later led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham)

steps.label: 2011 to 2012
steps.title: From protest to war
steps.text: Protests that began in Daraa in March 2011 spread across Syria and were met with live fire. Army defectors formed the Free Syrian Army, and by 2012 rebels held parts of Homs, Idlib and the Damascus suburbs. In July 2012 rebels pushed into Aleppo, which stayed divided for four years.

events.name: Daraa protests
events.text: Arrests of schoolboys sparked protests that spread nationwide.

events.name: Siege of Baba Amr, Homs
events.text: Government forces retook the rebel-held district after weeks of shelling.

events.name: Battle of Aleppo begins
events.text: Rebels seized the east of Syria's largest city.

steps.label: 2013 to 2014
steps.title: Hezbollah, chemical weapons and the Islamic State
steps.text: Hezbollah fighters helped government forces retake al-Qusayr in mid 2013, and a sarin attack on the Ghouta suburbs in August killed hundreds, leading to a deal to remove Syria's declared chemical arsenal. The Islamic State took Raqqa from other rebels in early 2014 and declared a caliphate in June. Its siege of Kurdish Kobani was broken in January 2015 by Kurdish YPG fighters backed by US air strikes.

fronts.label: Approx. western edge of Islamic State territory, 2014

events.name: Battle of al-Qusayr
events.text: The government and Hezbollah cut a rebel supply route from Lebanon.

events.name: Ghouta chemical attack
events.text: A sarin attack killed hundreds of people in rebel-held suburbs of Damascus.

events.name: Siege of Kobani
events.text: Kurdish YPG fighters and US air power held the town and the siege failed by January 2015.

steps.label: 2015 to 2016
steps.title: Russia intervenes
steps.text: A rebel coalition took Idlib in March 2015 and the Islamic State seized Palmyra in May, leaving the government at its weakest. From September 2015 Russian air power, Iranian-backed militias and Hezbollah turned the tide. In December 2016 government forces retook eastern Aleppo, the opposition's most important stronghold, after a long siege.

events.name: Fall of Idlib
events.text: A rebel coalition led by Islamist groups captured the provincial capital.

events.name: Russian air campaign begins
events.text: Russian jets began flying from Hmeimim air base on 30 September 2015.

events.name: Fall of eastern Aleppo
events.text: Remaining rebels and civilians were evacuated in December 2016.

steps.label: 2017 to 2019
steps.title: The caliphate falls
steps.text: The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, backed by the US-led coalition, took Raqqa in October 2017, while government forces broke the siege of Deir ez-Zor and advanced along the Euphrates. The government retook Eastern Ghouta and the south in 2018, and Turkey and allied rebels occupied areas of the north. The Islamic State lost its last village, Baghuz, in March 2019.

fronts.label: Euphrates line between government and SDF, 2018

events.name: Battle of Raqqa
events.text: The SDF took the Islamic State's capital after four months of fighting.

events.name: Fall of Eastern Ghouta
events.text: The last rebel enclave near Damascus surrendered in April 2018.

events.name: Battle of Baghuz
events.text: SDF forces ended the Islamic State's territorial control in March 2019.

steps.label: 2020 to 2023
steps.title: Frozen lines
steps.text: A government offensive in Idlib ended with a Russian-Turkish ceasefire in March 2020, leaving the northwest to Hayat Tahrir al-Sham and Turkish-backed factions. The country stayed divided among the government, the rebels, Turkish-held zones and the SDF in the northeast, while the economy collapsed. The Arab League readmitted Syria in 2023.

events.name: Moscow ceasefire
events.text: Russia and Turkey agreed a ceasefire along the M4 highway in Idlib.

events.name: Earthquake
events.text: The February 2023 earthquake killed thousands in northwest Syria.

steps.label: 27 Nov to 8 Dec 2024
steps.title: Fall of Assad
steps.text: On 27 November 2024 Hayat Tahrir al-Sham and allied factions under Ahmed al-Sharaa attacked from Idlib and took Aleppo within days, as government forces collapsed with Russia and Hezbollah distracted by other wars. Hama fell on 5 December and Homs on 7 December, while rebels in the south moved on Damascus. On 8 December rebels entered the capital and Assad fled to Moscow.

moves.label: South to Hama, Homs and Damascus

events.name: Capture of Aleppo
events.text: Rebels took Syria's second city almost without a fight.

events.name: Capture of Hama
events.text: Government forces withdrew from the city on 5 December.

events.name: Fall of Damascus
events.text: Assad's government fell on 8 December, ending more than 50 years of family rule.

name: Yemeni Civil War and Saudi-led Intervention
summary: The Houthi movement seized Sanaa in 2014 and pushed south, and in March 2015 a Saudi-led coalition intervened to restore President Hadi's government. The war settled into a stalemate that created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, and a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely ended the large-scale fighting. From late 2023 Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping drew strikes by the US, Britain and Israel, and Yemen remained divided at the end of 2025.

steps.label: Sep 2014 to Mar 2015
steps.title: The Houthis take Sanaa
steps.text: Houthi fighters from Saada, allied with forces loyal to former president Ali Abdullah Saleh, entered Sanaa in September 2014. In early 2015 they placed President Hadi under house arrest, and after he escaped to Aden they drove south toward the city.

events.name: Fall of Sanaa
events.text: Houthi forces took over the capital on 21 September 2014.

steps.label: Mar to Dec 2015
steps.title: Operation Decisive Storm
steps.text: On 26 March 2015 Saudi Arabia, led by defence minister Mohammed bin Salman, and its allies began air strikes and a naval blockade. UAE-backed southern forces retook Aden in July and pushed the Houthis out of most of the south, while fighting stalled around Marib and Taiz.

moves.label: Liberation of Aden and the south

events.name: Decisive Storm begins
events.text: Coalition air strikes hit Houthi positions across the north.

events.name: Battle of Aden
events.text: Southern fighters with Emirati support drove Houthi forces out of the city.

steps.label: 2016 to 2018
steps.title: Stalemate and the Hodeidah offensive
steps.text: Front lines barely moved as air strikes, the blockade, famine and cholera devastated the country. In December 2017 Saleh broke with the Houthis and was killed in Sanaa. In 2018 coalition-backed forces advanced up the Red Sea coast to Hodeidah, Yemen's main port, until the UN-brokered Stockholm Agreement halted the battle.

events.name: Death of Ali Abdullah Saleh
events.text: The former president was killed after turning against his Houthi allies.

events.name: Battle of Hodeidah
events.text: Coalition forces reached the city's edges but did not take the port.

events.name: Stockholm Agreement
events.text: The parties agreed a ceasefire in Hodeidah and a prisoner exchange.

steps.label: 2019 to 2021
steps.title: Rifts and the battle for Marib
steps.text: In August 2019 the separatist Southern Transitional Council, backed by the UAE, seized Aden from government forces, and the Riyadh Agreement later papered over the split. Houthi drones and missiles struck Saudi territory, including oil facilities at Abqaiq, which the Houthis claimed and the US blamed on Iran. From 2020 the Houthis attacked Marib, the government's last northern stronghold, but failed to take it.

events.name: Abqaiq and Khurais attacks
events.text: Strikes on Saudi oil plants briefly halved the kingdom's output.

events.name: Battle of Marib
events.text: Government forces backed by coalition air power held the city.

steps.label: 2022 to 2023
steps.title: Truce
steps.text: A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 paused air strikes and major offensives, and President Hadi handed power to a Presidential Leadership Council led by Rashad al-Alimi. The truce formally lapsed in October, but large-scale fighting did not resume, and Saudi Arabia held direct talks with the Houthis.

events.name: UN truce
events.text: A nationwide truce took effect on 2 April 2022.

steps.label: Nov 2023 to 2025
steps.title: Red Sea war and new rifts
steps.text: Saying they acted in support of Gaza, the Houthis attacked ships in the Red Sea and fired missiles at Israel from November 2023, prompting US and British strikes from January 2024 and Israeli strikes on Hodeidah and Sanaa. A US air campaign in 2025 ended in a May ceasefire between the US and the Houthis, and attacks largely stopped after the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire. In December 2025 the Southern Transitional Council moved to take control of much of eastern Yemen, straining the anti-Houthi camp.

events.name: Galaxy Leader seizure
events.text: Houthi forces hijacked a cargo ship by helicopter in November 2023.

events.name: US and UK strikes
events.text: Air and missile strikes on Houthi targets began on 12 January 2024.

events.name: US-Houthi ceasefire
events.text: An Oman-brokered deal in May 2025 ended US strikes and Houthi attacks on US ships.

name: Russia-Ukraine War
summary: Russia and Ukraine have been at war since 2014, when Russia annexed Crimea and backed armed separatists in the Donbas after Ukraine's pro-Western Euromaidan revolution. In February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion that failed to take Kyiv and became a war of attrition along a long front in the east and south. At the end of 2025 fighting continued without a ceasefire, in the largest war in Europe since 1945.

steps.label: Feb to Mar 2014
steps.title: Annexation of Crimea
steps.text: After protests in Kyiv led to the ouster of President Viktor Yanukovych, Russian troops without insignia took control of Crimea. A referendum held under Russian control, rejected as illegitimate by Ukraine and most UN members, was followed by Russia's annexation of the peninsula on 18 March 2014.

moves.commander: Black Sea Fleet and special forces
moves.label: Russian forces from Sevastopol

events.name: Annexation of Crimea
events.text: Russia declared the peninsula part of its territory on 18 March 2014.

steps.label: Apr 2014 to Feb 2015
steps.title: War in the Donbas
steps.text: Armed separatists backed by Russia, including a group under Igor Girkin, seized towns in Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, and Ukraine launched military operations against them. Ukrainian forces retook Sloviansk in July, but in August Russian regular units crossed the border and defeated them at Ilovaisk. The Minsk agreements of 2014 and 2015 froze but did not end the fighting.

moves.label: Separatists withdraw from Sloviansk to Donetsk

events.name: Recapture of Sloviansk
events.text: Separatist forces abandoned the town in July 2014.

events.name: Battle of Ilovaisk
events.text: Ukrainian units were encircled and suffered heavy losses during their withdrawal.

events.name: Battle of Debaltseve
events.text: Ukrainian forces withdrew from the rail hub days after the second Minsk agreement.

steps.label: 2015 to 2021
steps.title: A frozen front
steps.text: Trench warfare and shelling continued along a line of contact in the Donbas, and by early 2022 over 14,000 people had been killed since 2014. In 2018 Russian forces seized Ukrainian naval vessels near the Kerch Strait, and in 2021 Russia massed troops near Ukraine's borders.

events.name: Minsk II
events.text: A ceasefire and political roadmap that was never fully implemented.

events.name: Kerch Strait incident
events.text: Russian forces fired on and seized three Ukrainian naval vessels and their crews.

steps.label: Feb to Apr 2022
steps.title: Full-scale invasion
steps.text: On 24 February 2022 Russia invaded from Belarus, Russia and Crimea. Ukrainian forces under Oleksandr Syrskyi stopped the assault on Kyiv and Russia withdrew from the north by early April, but Russian troops took Kherson and much of the south and besieged Mariupol.

events.name: Battle of Kyiv
events.text: Ukrainian forces halted the Russian advance in the city's outskirts, and Russia withdrew from the north.

events.name: Battle of Kharkiv
events.text: Russian forces failed to take Ukraine's second-largest city.

events.name: Siege of Mariupol
events.text: Russian forces took the devastated city after the last defenders at the Azovstal steelworks surrendered in May.

steps.label: Sep to Nov 2022
steps.title: Ukrainian counteroffensives
steps.text: A rapid Ukrainian offensive led by Oleksandr Syrskyi recaptured most of Kharkiv oblast in September, and Russia announced a partial mobilisation and claimed to annex four Ukrainian oblasts, a claim most states reject. In November Russian forces under Sergei Surovikin withdrew across the Dnipro and Ukraine retook Kherson city.

events.name: Kharkiv counteroffensive
events.text: Ukrainian forces broke through and retook Izium, Kupiansk and thousands of square kilometres.

events.name: Recapture of Kherson
events.text: Russian forces withdrew from the only regional capital they had captured since February.

steps.title: Bakhmut and the summer counteroffensive
steps.text: Russian forces, led at Bakhmut by Wagner Group fighters under Yevgeny Prigozhin, captured the town in May after months of extremely costly fighting; in June Prigozhin briefly marched his men toward Moscow before standing down. Ukraine's summer counteroffensive in Zaporizhzhia oblast met dense minefields and made only small gains, and the Kakhovka dam was destroyed in June.

events.name: Battle of Bakhmut
events.text: Russian forces took the ruined city after about ten months of fighting.

events.name: Zaporizhzhia counteroffensive
events.text: Ukraine recaptured Robotyne and nearby villages but did not break the Russian defences.

events.name: Wagner mutiny
events.text: Wagner seized Rostov-on-Don and advanced north before a deal ended the revolt on 24 June.

steps.title: Avdiivka, Kursk and Pokrovsk
steps.text: Russia took Avdiivka in February and pressed slow, costly advances in Donetsk oblast toward Pokrovsk. In August Ukraine launched a surprise cross-border incursion into Russia's Kursk oblast, and North Korean troops were later deployed to help Russia push it back.

events.name: Battle of Avdiivka
events.text: Ukrainian forces withdrew from the heavily fortified town in February 2024.

events.name: Kursk incursion
events.text: Ukraine seized Sudzha and nearby areas; Russian forces retook most of the territory by March 2025.

steps.title: Attrition and diplomacy
steps.text: Russian forces pushed Ukraine out of Kursk oblast in the spring and continued slow advances in Donetsk oblast, fighting into Pokrovsk and Myrnohrad and pressing toward Kostiantynivka and Huliaipole, while both sides struck each other's cities, airfields and energy infrastructure with drones and missiles. US-led diplomacy produced talks, a Trump-Putin summit in Alaska and several peace proposals, but no ceasefire had been agreed by the end of 2025.

events.name: Kursk retaken
events.text: Russian and North Korean forces drove Ukrainian troops from Sudzha in March 2025.

events.name: Battle of Pokrovsk
events.text: Russian forces fought into the city through 2025; Russia claimed its capture late in the year.

events.name: Alaska summit
events.text: Trump and Putin met in Anchorage in August 2025 without agreeing a ceasefire.

name: Tigray War
summary: In November 2020 a power struggle between Ethiopia's federal government under Abiy Ahmed and the Tigray People's Liberation Front turned into war, with Eritrean and Amhara regional forces fighting alongside the federal army. Tigrayan forces retook their region in 2021 and advanced toward Addis Ababa before being driven back. The Pretoria peace agreement of November 2022 ended a war that killed hundreds of thousands, many through famine and blockade.

sides.name: Ethiopian federal government and allies (Eritrea, Amhara forces)
Tigray People's Liberation Front and Tigray Defence Forces

steps.label: Nov 2020
steps.title: Federal offensive
steps.text: After Tigrayan forces attacked federal Northern Command bases on 4 November 2020, Abiy Ahmed ordered an offensive. Federal troops and Amhara forces advanced from the south and west, Eritrean troops entered from the north, and Mekelle fell on 28 November as TPLF leaders withdrew into the mountains.

events.name: Northern Command attacks
events.text: Tigrayan forces seized federal army bases and weapons on 4 November.

events.name: Capture of Mekelle
events.text: Federal forces entered the Tigrayan capital and Abiy declared the operation over.

steps.label: Dec 2020 to Jun 2021
steps.title: Insurgency and the return to Mekelle
steps.text: Tigrayan forces regrouped in the countryside while reports of massacres, sexual violence and a blockade of aid drew international condemnation of all armed parties, especially Eritrean and federal forces. In June 2021 the Tigray Defence Forces under Tsadkan Gebretensae and Tadesse Werede counterattacked, and the government withdrew from Mekelle and declared a unilateral ceasefire.

events.name: Axum massacre
events.text: Human rights groups reported hundreds of civilians killed by Eritrean troops in late November 2020.

events.name: Recapture of Mekelle
events.text: Tigrayan forces re-entered the city on 28 June 2021.

steps.label: Jul to Nov 2021
steps.title: Advance toward Addis Ababa
steps.text: Tigrayan forces pushed south into Amhara and east into Afar, taking Lalibela, Dessie and Kombolcha and reaching Debre Sina, under 200 km from the capital. The government declared a state of emergency and mobilised militias, and Abiy announced he would lead from the front.

moves.label: Into Afar toward the Djibouti road

events.name: Capture of Dessie and Kombolcha
events.text: Tigrayan forces took the two towns at the start of November 2021.

steps.label: Dec 2021 to Jul 2022
steps.title: Federal counteroffensive and truce
steps.text: Backed by newly acquired armed drones, federal forces and allied militias drove the Tigrayan forces back into Tigray in December 2021. A humanitarian truce in March 2022 allowed some aid in, but Tigray remained cut off from banking, power and communications.

events.name: Recapture of Lalibela
events.text: Federal forces retook the town in December 2021 as Tigrayan forces retreated.

events.name: Humanitarian truce
events.text: The government declared a truce in March 2022 to allow aid deliveries.

steps.label: Aug to Nov 2022
steps.title: Final offensive and the Pretoria agreement
steps.text: Fighting resumed in August 2022, and federal and Eritrean forces took Shire, Axum and Adwa in October. On 2 November 2022 the government and the TPLF signed a cessation of hostilities in Pretoria, mediated by the African Union, providing for Tigrayan disarmament and restored services.

moves.label: Federal advance on Shire and Axum

events.name: Capture of Shire
events.text: Federal and Eritrean forces took the town in October 2022.

events.name: Pretoria Agreement
events.text: The African Union-brokered deal ended the war on 2 November 2022.

name: Sudanese Civil War
summary: In April 2023 a power struggle between the Sudanese Armed Forces under Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and the Rapid Support Forces under Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo (Hemedti) erupted into war in Khartoum. The RSF took most of the capital and Darfur, and the army later retook Khartoum and central Sudan, splitting the country between east and west. The war has killed tens of thousands and displaced over 10 million people, and it continued at the end of 2025.

steps.label: Apr to Sep 2023
steps.title: War in the capital
steps.text: On 15 April 2023 fighting broke out in Khartoum between the army and the RSF, former partners in the 2021 coup. RSF fighters seized much of the capital, while the army held key bases and used air power. Burhan left Khartoum in August and set up the government in Port Sudan, and mass killings of Masalit civilians were reported in El Geneina in West Darfur.

events.name: Battle of Khartoum begins
events.text: Heavy fighting erupted on 15 April across the capital and Omdurman.

events.name: El Geneina killings
events.text: The UN and rights groups reported thousands of Masalit civilians killed as the RSF took the city.

steps.label: Oct 2023 to Mar 2024
steps.title: RSF sweep Darfur and Gezira
steps.text: The RSF captured four of Darfur's five state capitals, including Nyala, in late 2023. In December they took Wad Madani, capital of the farming heartland of Gezira, and the war spread south and east. In early 2024 the army began a counteroffensive in Omdurman.

events.name: Fall of Nyala
events.text: The RSF took Sudan's second-largest city in October 2023.

events.name: Fall of Wad Madani
events.text: Army forces withdrew from the Gezira capital in December 2023.

steps.label: Apr to Dec 2024
steps.title: El Fasher and famine
steps.text: The RSF besieged El Fasher, the army's last stronghold in Darfur, from May 2024, and famine was confirmed in Zamzam displacement camp nearby. The RSF also advanced into Sennar state, while from September the army pushed across the Nile bridges into Khartoum.

events.name: Siege of El Fasher
events.text: The army and allied Darfuri forces held the city through 2024 under constant attack.

events.name: Famine in Zamzam
events.text: Famine was confirmed in the displacement camp in August 2024.

steps.label: Jan to May 2025
steps.title: The army retakes Khartoum
steps.text: The army recaptured Wad Madani in January 2025 and the presidential palace in central Khartoum in March, and by May the RSF had withdrawn from Khartoum state. The RSF answered with drone strikes on Port Sudan and moved to set up a rival government in the areas it held.

events.name: Recapture of Wad Madani
events.text: Army forces re-entered the Gezira capital on 11 January 2025.

events.name: Recapture of the presidential palace
events.text: The army took the palace in central Khartoum in March 2025.

steps.label: Jun to Dec 2025
steps.title: Fall of El Fasher and war in Kordofan
steps.text: After an 18-month siege, the RSF captured El Fasher in late October 2025, with widespread reports of mass killings of civilians, giving it control of nearly all of Darfur. Fighting shifted to Kordofan, where the RSF and its allies pressed on Babanusa, Kadugli and El Obeid. Sudan was effectively split between an army-held east and an RSF-held west, and diplomatic efforts had not produced a ceasefire.

events.name: Fall of El Fasher
events.text: The RSF took the city in late October 2025 amid reports of mass atrocities.

events.name: Battles in Kordofan
events.text: Kordofan became the main front at the end of 2025.

name: Israel-Hamas War
summary: On 7 October 2023 Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages, and Israel responded with an air and ground campaign in the Gaza Strip. The war killed tens of thousands of Palestinians, displaced most of Gaza's population and caused a severe humanitarian crisis, and it spread to Lebanon, Yemen and Iran. A US-brokered ceasefire in October 2025 returned the remaining living hostages, with Israeli troops still holding part of Gaza.

sides.name: Hamas and allied Palestinian armed groups

steps.label: 7 Oct 2023
steps.title: The 7 October attack
steps.text: Under rocket cover, thousands of militants led by Hamas's armed wing breached the Gaza border fence and attacked army posts, kibbutzim, towns and a music festival in southern Israel. About 1,200 people, most of them civilians, were killed and 251 taken into Gaza as hostages. Israel declared war and mobilised about 300,000 reservists.

events.name: Attack on Be'eri
events.text: More than 100 residents of the kibbutz were killed and dozens taken hostage.

events.name: Nova festival attack
events.text: Militants killed more than 360 people at the outdoor festival near Re'im.

steps.label: Oct to Dec 2023
steps.title: Invasion of northern Gaza
steps.text: After weeks of heavy bombardment and an order for civilians to move south, Israeli ground forces entered Gaza on 27 October, cut the strip in two along Wadi Gaza and encircled Gaza City. A week-long truce in late November exchanged 105 hostages for 240 Palestinian prisoners. In December the offensive turned south to Khan Yunis.

fronts.label: Israeli cordon along Wadi Gaza, Nov 2023

moves.label: Advance on Gaza City from the north

events.name: Siege of Gaza City
events.text: Israeli forces encircled the city and raided al-Shifa hospital in November.

events.name: November truce
events.text: Hostages and Palestinian prisoners were exchanged during a seven-day pause.

steps.label: Jan to Sep 2024
steps.title: Khan Yunis and Rafah
steps.text: Israeli forces fought through Khan Yunis until April 2024 and in May moved into Rafah, seizing the Philadelphi corridor along the Egyptian border. Most of Gaza's 2.1 million people were displaced, aid was severely limited, and the International Court of Justice ordered Israel to prevent acts of genocide and enable aid, which Israel said it was doing. Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh was killed in Tehran in July.

events.name: Battle of Khan Yunis
events.text: Israeli forces fought in Gaza's second city from December 2023 to April 2024.

events.name: Rafah offensive
events.text: Israel took Rafah and the border crossing with Egypt from May 2024.

steps.label: Sep to Dec 2024
steps.title: Sinwar killed, war in Lebanon
steps.text: Israel escalated its parallel conflict with Hezbollah, killing its leader Hassan Nasrallah in Beirut and sending troops into southern Lebanon until a ceasefire in November. In Gaza, Israeli troops killed Yahya Sinwar in a chance encounter in Rafah on 16 October and laid siege to Jabalia in the north.

events.name: Death of Yahya Sinwar
events.text: The Hamas leader was killed by Israeli troops in Tal al-Sultan.

events.name: Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire
events.text: A US and French-brokered ceasefire in Lebanon took effect on 27 November.

steps.label: Jan to Sep 2025
steps.title: Truce, collapse and Gaza City
steps.text: A ceasefire on 19 January 2025 returned 33 hostages in exchange for Palestinian prisoners, but it collapsed on 18 March when Israel resumed strikes and ground operations. A new US and Israeli-backed aid system began in May amid deadly crowding at distribution sites, and a UN-backed food security body declared famine in Gaza City in August. In September Israel launched an offensive to take Gaza City.

events.name: January ceasefire
events.text: A phased truce held for about two months.

events.name: Famine declared in Gaza City
events.text: The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification confirmed famine in August 2025.

steps.label: Oct to Dec 2025
steps.title: Ceasefire
steps.text: Under a US plan presented by President Trump, Israel and Hamas agreed a ceasefire that took effect on 10 October 2025. Hamas released the 20 remaining living hostages on 13 October and Israel freed about 2,000 Palestinian prisoners and detainees, while Israeli troops pulled back to a line leaving them in control of roughly half of Gaza. By then the Gaza Health Ministry reported over 67,000 Palestinians killed, and disarmament and Gaza's future governance remained unresolved.

events.name: October 2025 ceasefire
events.text: The truce took effect on 10 October after talks in Egypt.

events.name: Hostage and prisoner release
events.text: All living hostages returned to Israel on 13 October.

name: Twelve-Day War
summary: On 13 June 2025 Israel launched surprise air strikes on Iran's nuclear programme, military leaders and air defences, and Iran answered with waves of ballistic missiles and drones against Israel. On 22 June the United States bombed the nuclear sites at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan. A ceasefire took effect on 24 June, and the extent of lasting damage to Iran's nuclear programme remained disputed.

steps.label: 13 Jun 2025
steps.title: Operation Rising Lion
steps.text: Israeli aircraft and covertly placed drones struck air defences, missile launchers and the Natanz enrichment site, and killed armed forces chief Mohammad Bagheri, IRGC commander Hossein Salami and several nuclear scientists. Israel said it acted to stop Iran from building a nuclear weapon, which Iran denies seeking.

moves.label: Israeli Air Force strike on Tehran

events.name: Strike on Natanz
events.text: Israel hit the above-ground enrichment plant and power supply.

events.name: Strikes on Tehran
events.text: Senior commanders and scientists were killed in their homes and offices.

steps.label: 13 to 21 Jun 2025
steps.title: Missiles over Israel
steps.text: Iran fired hundreds of ballistic missiles and over a thousand drones at Israel; most were intercepted, but strikes hit Tel Aviv, Haifa, Beersheba and other cities. Israel gained air superiority over western Iran and Tehran and widened its strikes to missile bases, the Isfahan nuclear site, energy facilities and state broadcasting.

moves.commander: Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Aerospace Force
moves.label: Missile salvos at Israel
Strikes on Isfahan and missile bases

events.name: Missile strikes on Tel Aviv
events.text: Missiles that got through caused deaths and heavy damage in central Israel.

events.name: Soroka hospital hit
events.text: An Iranian missile damaged the Beersheba hospital on 19 June.

events.name: Strike on Isfahan
events.text: Israel hit uranium conversion facilities at Isfahan.

steps.label: 22 Jun 2025
steps.title: Operation Midnight Hammer
steps.text: US B-2 bombers flew from Missouri and dropped 14 bunker-buster bombs on the deeply buried Fordow enrichment site and on Natanz, while a submarine fired Tomahawk missiles at Isfahan. President Trump said the sites had been destroyed, while later assessments of the damage differed.

moves.label: B-2 bombers from Whiteman Air Force Base

events.name: Strike on Fordow
events.text: Twelve GBU-57 bombs hit the enrichment plant built inside a mountain.

steps.label: 23 to 24 Jun 2025
steps.title: Retaliation and ceasefire
steps.text: Iran fired missiles at the US Al Udeid air base in Qatar after giving advance warning, and nearly all were intercepted without casualties. President Trump then announced a ceasefire, which took effect on 24 June after a final exchange of strikes. Iranian authorities reported about 1,000 people killed in Iran, and about 30 were killed in Israel.

moves.commander: Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Aerospace Force
moves.label: Missiles at Al Udeid

events.name: Attack on Al Udeid
events.text: Iran's symbolic strike on the US base caused no casualties.

events.name: Ceasefire
events.text: The truce announced by Trump took effect on 24 June and held.
